articles.title: Mirwaiz says he was put under house arrest over Vande Mataram issue, decries action against Maulana Qasimi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Friday (November 27, 2026) said he was placed under house arrest and another prominent cleric, Maulana Rehmatullah Qasimi, was summoned to a police station over their opposition to the playing of Vande Mataram at a J&K Waqf Board function in Srinagar.

“I had anticipated that I would be punished this Friday by being put under house arrest. I also raised concerns over the recitation of Vande Mataram at the religious function of the J&K Waqf Board, as well as people’s grave concerns over the disaster-in-waiting in the ecologically fragile region of Sheshnag after the viral visuals,” the Mirwaiz said in a statement.
The Mirwaiz alleged he was “prevented from proceeding to Jama Masjid, Srinagar, to deliver the Friday sermon and offer congregational prayers.”
“It has become a precedent that every time I raise people’s issues and concerns, I am not allowed to go to Jama Masjid on that Friday,” the Mirwaiz said.
The chief cleric also expressed “deep regret” over the summoning of Mr. Qasimi, head of Kashmir’s largest seminary, Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, in Bandipora.
Mr. Qasimi also spoke about the playing of Vande Mataram during the J&K Waqf Board Day on November 23 in Srinagar, which was attended by local imams and religious scholars.

“Yesterday (Thursday), Kashmir’s renowned Islamic scholar and patron of the Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulama, Maulana Rehmatullah Qasimi Sahib, was summoned to the police station and reprimanded. Can we no longer raise our voices to safeguard our religious beliefs and sentiments? Do we not even have the right to express our religious concerns?” the Mirwaiz said.
He added that those in power must understand that “we will not tolerate any coercion in matters of faith, particularly when it comes to our fundamental belief in Tawheed.”

“It would serve the ruling regime much better if, instead of applying pressure on me, it understands the sensitivity and impact these issues have on the people of J&K. It should desist from imposing things that cause people hurt and concern,” the Mirwaiz said.

Meanwhile, Kashmir’s Grand Mufti Nasir-ul-Islam on Thursday (November 26, 2026) stated, “Reciting Vande Mataram and attending related ceremonies is not permissible under Islamic law. The act is wrong and unacceptable. Such actions should not be defended under any circumstances.”
Earlier, a number of Muslim clerics tendered apologies and offered special repentance prayers for attending the Waqf function where Vande Mataram was played.

articles.title: Why Delimitation Bill failed to pass in Parliament in April 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A special parliamentary sitting has been announced on November 30, 2026, bringing renewed focus to the delimitation debate after more than 100 days without prorogation following the August 13 monsoon adjournment.

The Union government is set to bring an amended Delimitation Bill that proposes a uniform 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats, extends the 1971 Census freeze on state seat shares for 25 years and uses the 2011 Census to redraw constituencies within each state.

The legislation failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha when it was put to a vote in April 2026, with the opposition citing concerns about the government’s move to link women’s reservation with delimitation based on the 2011 Census. They also pointed out the absence of a clear guarantee that the representation of all States in the Lok Sabha would increase uniformly by 50%, as the government had claimed.
Why the numbers matter in the renewed push for delimitation | Explained
Delimitation: how to align what is said and what is written

Delimitation is the process of fixing the number of seats and boundaries of the territorial constituencies in each State for the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies. This ‘Delimitation process’ is performed by a higher-power body called the ‘Delimitation Commission’ that is set up under an act of Parliament. Such exercises have previously been conducted based on the 1951, 1961, and 1971 Censuses. The last time the number of seats was determined was on the basis of 1971 census population.

The current Delimitation Bill aims to significantly expand the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats (815 from States, 35 from Union Territories), acknowledging the substantial population growth in India based on the latest census figures. This bill will officially end the 50-year “freeze” on reallocating seats between States, allowing for a redistribution based on current population trends. Opposition have voiced concern that the exercise could have significant consequences for political power and influence at both the State and National levels.

In April, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill failed to win two-thirds of the majority to amend the Constitution. Out of 528 members present and voting in the Lok Sabha, 298 voted in favour and 230 voted against, falling short of the 352 votes needed.
Because the constitutional amendment did not pass, the government shelved the companion Delimitation Bill and Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, stating they could not be viewed in isolation

A major concern back in April was how seats would be allocated across states. The tabled text linked delimitation to the latest published census, which was the 2011 census, rather than writing a guaranteed proportional seat share into the bill. Following through with it would have reduced the share of southern, eastern, and northeastern states due to their lower population growth relative to the Hindi heartland states.
Home Minister Amit Shah offered a verbal assurance of a 50% pro rata increase and floated redrafting it, but the opposition rejected this since the written text pointed elsewhere.

Opposition parties also objected to tying one-third reservation for women to delimitation and rushing the package through Parliament. Under the 106th Constitutional Amendment passed in 2023, women’s reservation was linked to delimitation following the next census , whereas the 131st Amendment proposed raising the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850 and linking women’s quota implementation to delimitation based on the 2011 census.

articles.title: Punjab polls: SAD, BJP reunification puts both parties back in the reckoning
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The reunification of the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) ahead of the crucial 2027 Punjab Assembly election has put both parties back in the reckoning, even as the State’s political landscape looks headed for a four-cornered fight, with the old partners joining hands to make it more competitive.

In the run-up to the election, due in early 2027, the political positioning of the parties appeared increasingly vulnerable, and political observers felt that the logical way to overcome it was to forge an alliance.

articles.title: Blistering heat, soaring UV levels and high humidity keep Kerala on its toes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Blistering heat, soaring ultraviolet (UV) levels, oppressive humidity amplified by rising heat index values, and the urban heat island effect are making life increasingly uncomfortable across Kerala during the peak of the summer with residents reporting unease amid the sweltering, sultry conditions, which are expected to persist until the first week of May.
Visual story: How this year’s El Niño hit India’s farms

Temperatures crossed the 40˚C mark twice last week in Palakkad and are now dangerously hovering around heatwave threshold levels at many stations across the State, especially in Punalur and Palakkad. Coastal regions in north Kerala, including Kannur and Kozhikode, have also been experiencing sultry conditions due to unusually high relative humidity in the air, which drives the ‘feels-like’ temperature dangerously high.

The latest weather bulletin issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Friday warned of above-average temperatures across the State. The agency has forecast maximum temperatures of around 40˚C at isolated places in Palakkad district, 39˚C in Kollam district, 38˚C in Kottayam district, 37˚C in Alappuzha, Pathanamthitta, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Kannur, and Kasaragod districts, and 36˚C in Thiruvananthapuram district (2 to 3˚C above normal) until April 19.

In addition, the rising mercury levels have put many regions in the State at high risk from UV rays, with several places recording alarming levels of radiation this season, according to Dr. M.G. Manoj, a scientist with the Advanced Centre for Atmospheric Radar Research (ACARR) at Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT).

Data recorded by the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) show that UV Index (UVI) values of 8–9, classified as “very high,” pose significant risks of sunburn, skin damage, and eye problems, Mr. Manoj said. This rise in UV levels, coupled with the urban heat island (UHI) effect, which makes temperatures in densely populated cities as much as 2˚C higher than in rural areas, makes life more difficult in urban regions. Materials used in constructing buildings, roads, and roofs, such as concrete, asphalt (tar), and bricks do not transmit light and have higher heat capacity and thermal conductivity, driving the temperatures up in the urban areas, making hot and humid conditions uncomfortable during summer.

However, according to IMD sources, a heatwave is unlikely to occur in Kerala this year as a weak La Niña, a climate pattern characterised by colder-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, is prevailing. It is expected that by the end of this month, summer rainfall will increase, preventing temperatures from reaching heatwave levels like those experienced in Kerala in 2024 during the El Niño period, the opposite of La Niña, which suppresses rainfall and causes dryness in the Indian subcontinent.

For a heatwave to be declared, the maximum temperature should be 40°C or more (for plains), with a departure from normal of at least 4.5°C. For coastal regions, the maximum temperature should be greater than or equal to 37°C, with a departure from normal of 4.5°C. Additionally, such conditions must be recorded at least at two stations for two consecutive days, as stipulated by the IMD. This is unlikely under the present conditions, as departures from normal have mostly remained within the range of 1–3°C so far this season, according to scientists.

articles.title: NGT-appointed amicus report flags gaps in Keralam’s solid, liquid waste management
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A report filed by an amicus curiae appointed by the National Green Tribunal (NGT) has flagged multiple gaps in the management of solid and liquid waste in Keralam.

The deficiencies have been pointed out in the observation note dated November 24, 2026 submitted in the matter related to the compliance of Municipal Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 and other environmental issues in the State. The amicus curiae made the observations based on the affidavits and compliance reports submitted by the authorities.

The report stated that about four-fifths of sanitary waste is not scientifically treated. Only 42.1 tonnes per day of the total sanitary waste of 203.66 tonnes generated daily is treated. Even when all projects are complete, the capacity will be 113.25 tonnes per day, it said.

The amicus curiae pointed out that inert waste is being used for land filling without safeguards. Quoting a report submitted by the Keralam government, the report said that about 404.8 tonnes per day of inert waste is used for filling up appropriate portions of hilly areas, stadiums, railway platforms, yards and road embankment formations. No register of sites, test reports or approvals is given. Given the State’s wetlands and landslide-prone slopes, this practice needs strict control, it suggested.

The report said that the action on the illegal drains discharging untreated sewage into streams and water bodies has been initiated in only four districts, including Kollam, Ernakulam, Alappuzha and Kottayam as per the affidavit submitted by the government. Of the 723 illegal outlets in the four districts, 671 are in Ernakulam alone.

The total quantity of processed and unprocessed legacy (old) waste has increased from 19.54 lakh metric tonnes in December 2025 to 19,6 lakh metric tonnes in July 2026. The gap in total sewage generated and treated is as high as 3901.2 million litres daily, indicative of a serious concern, it said.

The amicus curiae has suggested a sample-based functional audit of composting bins and biogas plants. The four regional plants for sanitary waste treatment should be commissioned by a fixed date. For inert and land filling, a register of every site where inert are used for filling be maintained and published, with test reports and approvals.
The report suggested preparation of a GIS-mapped inventory of drains, streams and storm-water channels carrying sewage into rivers, backwaters, ponds and the sea.

articles.title: 34% monsoon deficit, bleak August outlook set alarm bells ringing in Kerala
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: As the southwest monsoon has crossed the halfway mark, Kerala is staring at a bleak season, with rainfall recording a deficit of around 34% during the first two months of the four-month monsoon season. The first two months typically account for around 65% of the total seasonal rainfall. However, by the end of July, the State had received only 853.8 mm of rainfall against the normal 1,301.7 mm for the period, a deficit of 34%.
Visual story: How this year’s El Niño hit India’s farms

Adding to the concern, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast below-normal rainfall for Kerala in August, which typically receives an average of 445.2 mm of rainfall during a normal monsoon, followed by 271.7 mm in September. This means that only an exceptionally large surplus in August and September could offset the deficit recorded during the peak monsoon months of June and July.

If the latest forecast and prevailing synoptic conditions are any indication, the State appears to be heading towards a drought year, particularly if the monsoon remains weak in August and September. Global weather models and prevailing synoptic conditions are not favourable for any significant enhancement of rainfall over Kerala during August.

Speaking to The Hindu , Neetha K. Gopal, Director of the IMD, Thiruvananthapuram, said that after two days of moderate to heavy rainfall, the monsoon is expected to slip into a lull phase. It is likely to show brief signs of revival towards the end of the first week of August, coinciding with the formation of a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. However, the anticipated position and track of the system are not favourable for any substantial increase in rainfall over Kerala. After this, the State is likely to witness a relatively prolonged dry spell, she said.

In addition, the expected peak of El Niño, the periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean that tends to weaken the Indian monsoon, during August and September, coupled with the persistence of neutral Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) conditions, has diminished the prospects of good monsoon rainfall during the remainder of the season. There is a slight possibility that the IOD could turn positive towards the end of September, which could improve monsoon prospects. However, it remains to be seen whether it would be strong enough to minimise the impact of the anticipated strong El Niño, Ms. Gopal said.

During the last El Niño year (2023–24), India, including Kerala, witnessed one of the driest Augusts on record. Kerala received only 86 mm of rainfall against the normal 445.2 mm during the month. The summer that followed also witnessed record-breaking temperatures, with Kerala experiencing a heat wave for the first time in its recorded history.

articles.title: The fiscal cost of cash-transfer schemes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Business Standard reported on May 13, 2026 that “Cash-transfer promises have moved from the margins of Indian election manifestos to the centre of political competition, with parties across States promising monthly or one-time payments.” Quoting a PRS Legislative Research report, it further said, “12 States are expected to spend nearly ₹1.68 trillion on unconditional cash-transfer schemes for women in 2025-26, … the outgo is roughly equivalent to 0.5 per cent of India’s GDP, compared with less than 0.2 per cent two years ago.”

The RBI report ‘State Finance: Study of State Budgets 2025-26’ reported that the total subsidy outlay increased from ₹1.87 trillion in 2018-19 to ₹4.26 trillion in 2025-26. States often implement promises from their election manifestos soon after forming the government and just before the next election, without any serious assessment of needs or financial commitments.

Conception and funding of an infrastructure project are guided by a Detailed Project Report (DPR) that specifies objectives, alternatives considered, financial and economic analysis, risk mitigation, baseline data, and success criteria. A social policy, by contrast, is often the outcome of an electoral promise or based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any comparable ex ante appraisal. Social policies affect human capabilities more directly than infrastructure projects.

The scarcity of public resources and their alternative uses make ex ante appraisal of social sector schemes essential. Moreover, social policies are vulnerable to electoral clientelism, and should therefore adhere to the same principles of public expenditure as infrastructure projects — evidence, accountability, equity, efficiency and fiscal responsibility as infrastructure. The claim that the benefits of social policies are not quantifiable should not stop ex ante appraisal, as methodologies exist to overcome this barrier.

An ex ante appraisal of a social project leaves an audit trail: the legislature, auditors, the media, and citizens can ask whether the project delivered what it promised. Many social schemes are implemented without the assessment of needs, identification of potential beneficiaries, or adequate funding, and a bureaucratic, top-down, target-chasing approach often replaces a democratic, bottom-up planning and implementation process.
This article explores the fiscal and economic fallout of cash transfers and universal subsidies.

If politics decides the desired social ends of such schemes, public finance and administration should decide the programme’s funding priority, the quantum of funding and the implementation process required to achieve those ends.

Prioritising expenditure is the first step in checking the desirability of public expenditure. For example, the Government of Tamil Nadu allocated nearly ₹1,000 crore in 2026-27 to provide scholarships for girls and boys from Government schools to continue higher education. A recent report in a Tamil Magazine ( Ananda Vikatan , November 18, 2026), based on replies it received to RTI applications, found 7,198 vacancies in permanent teaching positions in Government Arts and Science Colleges. If we include teacher vacancies in professional colleges and universities, the number should be nearly 9,000. Filling these vacancies, delayed for over a decade, would cost ₹1,080 crore per annum, rising every year thereafter. With a huge revenue deficit and fiscal deficit, the State budget lacks the revenue cushion to spend an additional ₹1,080 crore per annum. Prioritising is a normative decision: filling vacancies ensures students learn from regular teachers, whereas funding scholarships alone sends them to colleges without regular teachers.

Deciding the quantum of funding and the process of execution requires ex ante evaluation. This should be explicitly oriented toward designing programmes that maximise impact for a given cost, using behavioural models and micro-simulations to predict the effects of hypothetical programmes before implementation.

For instance, a universal subsidy scheme is a trade-off between inclusion and exclusion errors. If it is truly universal, the scheme commits the error of including the undeserving and thus reduces the per-capita benefit to people in need. In a target-oriented scheme, it commits the error of excluding the deserving, but it increases the per-capita benefit to people in need. The choice between the two requires ex ante appraisal of such schemes.

Cash transfers and subsidies are perpetual in nature as they are politically hard to reverse. Therefore, the continuous commitment of scarce financial resources demands not only prior evaluation but also real-time monitoring and evaluation to redesign and right-size schemes.

In practice, fiscal constraints are addressed through post-hoc adjustments, usually by increasing borrowing or cutting even essential public expenditure. Fiscal constraints should, however, prompt more disciplined choices.

articles.title: Experts say new U.S. tariffs do not pose substantial threat, India should not rush into trade deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The tariffs are not final yet, with the U.S. government opening a window for written comments and requests to testify by January 5, 2027. Public hearings will begin on January 25, 2027, following which the final action will be communicated.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

The president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Anil Gupta, pointed out that the tariffs will have a limited impact on Indian exports due to the nature of the commodities that India predominantly exports to the U.S.

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.
“Strong bank and non-bank credit growth continues to support the domestic economy. Further, sustained double-digit export growth broadened the base of economic expansion,” they added.
Equity markets remained buoyant amid robust corporate earnings and foreign portfolio investment inflows, while net inflows through external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits remained strong.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

articles.title: Duty-free raw sugar imports up to 10 lakh tonnes allowed till March 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar will be permitted until the end of March 2027, according to a notification issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) on Wednesday.

A notification issued on August 20 had allowed duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of sugar under the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) scheme until December 31, 2026. Separately, the DGFT has allowed sugar mills time until September 30, 2027, to process the imported raw sugar and sell it in the domestic market.

The Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association Director General Deepak Ballani told The Hindu that price parity had prevailed over the past, making it viable for Indian importers to source raw sugar from international markets, primarily Brazil. Some imports have already begun.

The industry expects more imports in the coming days and this will ensure supply of adequate quantity of sugar in the domestic market throughout the sugar season. It will also keep the prices stable, he said.

articles.title: Air passenger services see 35% inflation in Q2; banking, securities transaction witness deflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.
The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.
Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.
As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.
Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.
Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.
Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.
The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

The government in June came out with the maiden PPI data for both goods and services to better reflect price movement at producer's level, paving the way for phasing out wholesale price index (WPI)-based inflation numbers in the next five years. Thereafter, in August the services PPI data was issued.

articles.title: Hasina has become a ‘thorn’ in Bangladesh-India ties: Minister Humaiun Kobir
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Sheikh Hasina has become a “thorn” in Bangladesh-India relations, with New Delhi beginning to realise the strain her presence in the country is causing to bilateral ties, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has said.

Comparing the deposed Prime Minister to an unwelcome guest who suddenly walks into someone’s home, Mr. Kobir said India was in a difficult position as it could neither send her away nor avoid dealing with her presence, news portal bdnews24 reported.
Read more: Sheikh Hasina’s return gambit tests Bangladesh’s political fault lines
“Hasina has become a thorn in Bangladesh-India relations,” he told reporters at the Foreign Ministry on Thursday (November 26, 2026).
“She has become an irritation, and they understand that this is a problem for the relationship,” Mr. Kobir said.
His remarks came a day after India refrained from commenting on Ms. Hasina’s plan to return to Bangladesh on December 16.

External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) said that her voluntary return should be treated separately from Dhaka’s extradition request, which New Delhi was examining through established legal processes.
Mr. Kobir reiterated that Ms. Hasina could return only under the extradition treaty between India and Bangladesh, either in handcuffs or under strict surveillance.

“She is a criminal. There is one policy for criminals and another for ordinary citizens. She falls under the criminal category. She will come only through the extradition treaty. It is not a matter of her returning; she will be handed over,” he said.
Ms. Hasina’s presence in India has emerged as a contentious issue in bilateral ties since her departure from Bangladesh.
She faces serious legal challenges in her home country, including a death sentence handed down in absentia by a special tribunal over the deadly crackdown on protesters during the 2024 uprising.
Ms. Hasina has denied wrongdoing and questioned the legitimacy of the proceedings.

articles.title: Pakistan set to host talks with Saudi Arabia, Turkey under trilateral defence pact
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Pakistan is set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday (November 27, 2026) under a trilateral defence pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three, two security officials said.

The talks in Islamabad will focus on developments in West Asia, including ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels , the officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the meeting publicly.

Pakistan has said that the agreement is purely defensive in nature and not against anyone, including Iran, and that the trilateral alliance reflects a shared desire to strengthen strategic security cooperation.

Senior diplomats as well as defence and military officials from the three countries are expected to discuss ways to deter threats, expand military cooperation, share intelligence and strengthen defence industry ties, the officials said. Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif, Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will attend the meeting.
Mr. Asif has said that Pakistan will use “whatever means are available” to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks from the Houthis.

However, Pakistan is still making efforts, with help from countries in West Asia, including Qatar, to urge the United States and Iran to return to the negotiating table to end the conflict in the region and beyond through talks. Pakistan had brokered an interim deal between the two sides in June 2026.

Friday’s meeting of the Strategic, Political and Defense Committee falls under the Joint Mecca Defense Agreement, which was signed in August 2026 in the Saudi holy city of Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

Pakistan’s government has not released details ahead of the meeting, but the authorities have declared a local holiday in Islamabad to limit public movement as part of security measures for the gathering. Islamabad traffic police have announced road diversions and advised motorists to use alternative routes to accommodate the movement of foreign delegations.

During a previous meeting in Riyadh, the three sides had vowed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defence commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed-upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.

According to the agreement, the group’s secretariat has been established in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani General Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will also attend Friday’s meeting. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, after which they would need to give three months’ notice before leaving.

articles.title: Costa Rica bars entry to UN rapporteur over ‘links to terrorist acts’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Costa Rica's government said on Thursday (November 26, 2026) it had denied entry to UN rapporteur Francesca Albanese, who has accused Israel of genocide, because she was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts."

Ms. Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, arrived on Thursday (November 26) at the airport serving the capital, San Jose, to receive an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica, a public university.

Ms. Albanese "is the subject of an international alert over links to terrorist acts," Omer Badilla, director general of Costa Rica's immigration authority, which falls under the interior ministry, said in a video posted on social media.
"I hope this clears up any doubts and makes clear the threat this woman poses to national security," he added.

The rector's office at the institution, the country's most important and prestigious university, said in a statement that immigration authorities were "blocking" Ms. Albanese's entry and asked the government to explain the decision.
The government of Costa Rican President Laura Fernández is a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump and has pursued closer trade ties with Israel since she took office in May.

Last December, Ms. Albanese criticised a free trade agreement between Costa Rica and Israel and called for its ratification to be put on hold, prompting a rebuke from the government, which accused her of interfering in domestic affairs.
The United States, Israel's main ally, imposed sanctions on Ms. Albanese after she criticised Washington's policy on Gaza.
"You see the face of empire the day you touch a nerve or cross its boundaries," Ms. Albanese wrote from the airport.

The university said it was awarding the honorary doctorate, which it grants annually to a prominent figure, in recognition of her "solid academic background, experience, publications and work exposing wrongdoing."

The Italian independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her longstanding accusations that Israel has committed genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, welcomed Costa Rica's decision.

articles.title: Canada’s top court rules on Quebec secularism law in landmark case
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The Supreme Court rules on Friday (November 27, 2026) on one of Canada's most closely watched cases -- a Quebec law barring some provincial employees from wearing religious symbols.
The law has been the subject of intense legal debate since it was first passed by Quebec's government in 2019.

That is partly due to the implications for Quebec, a majority French-speaking province where the decades-long battle to enforce secularism is a core issue and where the Catholic Church once wielded enormous influence over public life.

The case reflects a conflict playing out elsewhere in the world as strictly secular states such as that of France face pressure typical of the Anglo-Saxon world for people to be able to practice their religion freely, including wearing whatever symbols of it that they wish.
The Quebec case is also seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the so-called "notwithstanding clause."
That clause, a quirk of Canada's legal system, effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution, known as the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Quebec pre-emptively invoked the "notwithstanding clause" when passing its secularism bill, anticipating it would be challenged over constitutional protections guaranteeing freedom of religion and expression.
Conservative-led provinces have also invoked the clause to defend legislation relating to transgender youth.
In 2023, Saskatchewan used the clause to pass a law requiring schools to obtain parental consent before changing the pronouns used for children under 16.
Alberta has also invoked the clause in relation to laws banning transgender girls from participating in female sports and restricting hormone therapy for individuals under 16.
The Supreme Court's ruling in the Quebec case will be scrutinized for potential national impact.
It says public employees in certain positions of authority, such as judges, police officers and teachers, cannot wear religious symbols.

fullParagraphs: AirAsia has ‌told employees it will delay salary payments to the end of each month ​from November through March, according to an internal email seen by Reuters , as ⁠the airline takes measures to conserve cash and its Philippine unit cuts jobs.

The email, sent to Malaysia-based staff late last week by Chief People Officer Muhammad Khurram Zia, cited the need for a “temporary operational adjustment” at ‌Southeast Asia’s largest budget airline, which like its peers faces higher jet fuel costs.
Salary payments during the five-month period would be made on the 30th of each month ‌or the last day of February, the email said.
It cited a “challenging environment” and asked employees ‌for “patience ⁠and flexibility.”
The email’s contents were confirmed by two people familiar with the matter. ⁠One of the people said AirAsia had previously paid salaries earlier in the second half of each month.

U.S. low-cost ‌carrier Spirit Airlines collapsed in May, Latvia’s airBaltic sought bankruptcy protection in September and Norway’s Norse Atlantic suspended flights on Thursday as it looks for urgent short-term financing.
Shares in AirAsia, which employs about 26,000 people predominantly in Asia, have declined more than 70% ‌this year as elevated fuel prices and foreign exchange losses squeezed its operations.
AirAsia Philippines said ​on Thursday (November 26, 2026) it would reduce its workforce following sustained pressure on its operating costs, without specifying how many staff would be affected.

The airline said on Friday (November 27) it ⁠remained fully operational and committed to serving the Philippine market. The planned workforce adjustment will not affect passenger flights, bookings, or other services, AirAsia Philippines General Manager and President Anna Victoria Lu said in a ‌statement.
The AirAsia Philippines Pilots’ Union filed notice of a strike after 90 pilots were retrenched, its president said in a video posted on social media on Thursday (November 26).

articles.title: 200-year-old Taj Mahal marble slab to be auctioned in U.K.
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: An intricate floral-bordered marble slab taken from the Taj Mahal in Agra by an officer of the East India Company is set to be auctioned in the U.K. next month.

The rectangular slab, one of two that Colonel Pownoll Phipps collected in 1816 at the end of his tenure as superintendent of the repairs of the buildings in and around Agra, is estimated to fetch between 20,000 and 30,000 pounds (₹24-36 lakh approximately).
It is being offered as part of the Islamic and Indian Art sale by Lyon and Turnbull auctioneers on December 9.

“The marble slab is accompanied by a vintage black and white photograph of the Taj Mahal and two letters — one printed by the grandson of Colonel Pownoll and one handwritten by the Marquess of Bath,” the auction notes state.

The colonel’s son's memoirs quote that his father found them in a ‘souterrain’, or underground area, at the Taj Mahal and that he thought they were intended for the repairs to the iconic Mughal-era monument.
Colonel Pownoll Phipps was born in Devon, England, in 1780. Hailing from a line of soldiers since the early 17th century, he joined the East India Company as a cadet in the Bengal Army in 1799.

After battling troops in Egypt, Phipps returned to India, where he quickly rose through the ranks, becoming Fort-Adjutant and Barrack-Master at Agra in 1809, where he remained for the next seven years.
During the colonial era, he was responsible among other things for the care of the Taj Mahal and other historic buildings.

“He took this job most seriously and was at times called upon to prevent damage by Europeans looking for keepsakes. As his son wrote, ‘he was once sent for to the Taj, where, in spite of the remonstrances of the sentry, an English lady was insisting on picking agates out of the marble with a steel fork’,” the auctioneers note.
In 1816, the colonel was chosen by the Governor General of India to become Superintendent of Building in the Lower Provinces, which meant leaving Agra for Kolkata.
His interest in the art and architecture of India remained, however, and he maintained “a staff of very skilful native draughtsmen” who made detailed images of the buildings under his care.
He and his family returned to Britain in 1823, and he died there in 1858. The slab was in the family’s collection for over 200 years.

fullParagraphs: MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, has launched an AI-powered MRI facility, offering specialised imaging services for neurological, cardiac, musculoskeletal, spinal, and other conditions.
The facility was inaugurated by J. Radhakrishnan, Chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission, on Thursday (November 26, 2026).

The system uses deep learning algorithms to correct motion-related artefacts and improve image quality, potentially reducing the need for repeat scans. It also offers specialised fetal and breast MRI, cardiac MRI, whole-body imaging, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and perfusion imaging.

According to the hospital, the technology can also reduce scan time. A brain MRI that conventionally takes about 35 minutes can now be completed in under 14 minutes. This could benefit patients who find it difficult to remain still for prolonged periods due to pain or discomfort.

Thinesh Ram, senior consultant and head of Imaging and Interventional Radiology, MGM Healthcare Malar, said the system would enable more detailed evaluation of neural pathways and expand the range of diagnostic assessments.

S. Kripanandh, chief operating officer, MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, and group chief business officer, said the facility would strengthen the hospital’s diagnostic capabilities and expand access to advanced imaging services in the neighbourhood.

articles.title: Elevated blood sugar during adulthood linked with worse cognition in midlife: study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Young adults with progressively increasing fasting blood sugar may be more likely to have a poor cognitive functioning by midlife, according to a new study that tracked young adults for over three decades.
The findings suggest that changes in glucose metabolism may affect brain health earlier in adulthood than previously thought.
Participants who developed type 2 diabetes during the study also showed signs of structural brain changes, according to findings published in the Journal of the American Heart Association .

"Diabetes is known to affect cognitive function, but cognitive impairment due to diabetes was once believed to happen mostly during childhood among people with Type 1 diabetes or after age 65 in people with Type 2 diabetes," lead author Regina Paradela, a post-doctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School in São Paulo, Brazil, said.

"However, prediabetes and sustained elevated fasting blood sugar levels in adults without type 1 or type 2 diabetes may also have an increased risk of late-life cognitive decline and dementia," Paradela said.
The researchers suggested early monitoring and management of blood sugar levels in young adulthood -- 18 to 30 years old -- might be a strategy to preserve brain health.

Normal fasting blood glucose is generally below 100 milligrams per decilitre, 100-125 milligrams per decilitre indicates prediabetes and a value over 126 milligrams per decilitre is consistent with Type 2 diabetes.

"The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very important," Paradela said.
"This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about," Paradela said.

The study is among the first to investigate and compare the association between changes in fasting blood sugar levels from early adulthood to changes in cognition and brain structure in middle age, over approximately 30 years, the researchers said.

Health data for nearly 3,000 participants in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which enrolled Black and white adults aged 18 to 30 in four US cities from 1985 to 1986, was analysed. MRI brain scans were taken for 605 participants.

Researchers identified three fasting blood sugar trajectories from young adulthood to midlife: lower-stable glucose (blood sugar), moderate-stable glucose and increasing glucose. About 345 participants developed diabetes during the 30-year follow-up.

articles.title: Parenting in an anxious age: What does ‘good enough’ look like?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Prem Kishore occasionally turns to Artificial Intelligence (AI) for help when it comes to raising his six-year-old son. “It’s the big feelings that can be difficult to talk about, because we don’t always have the right words. I usually seek advice from my friends or psychologists, but if they’re not available, I turn to AI,” says the creative professional, 43, who splits his time between Bengaluru and Dubai.
Kishore recalls how he visited an AI video generator to create an avatar of a doctor, who chatted with his son about healthy boundaries and consent.

As AI becomes more enmeshed in our day-to-day lives, families are turning to it for advice, research and assistance in managing the mental load of modern-day parenting. A 2026 consumer trends report by GIPSI, the research arm of agency Tonic Worldwide, combined search and social media data with a survey of 50,000 people, and found that 52% of Indian Gen Z parents now use AI instead of their usual search engines, and 48% use it as an adviser. In India, Google Gemini recently launched a series of commercials featuring Shah Rukh Khan in which he directs two fathers at very different stages of their parenting journeys towards the chatbot for advice. Apps such as Fambot and AVA seek to help families with administrative tasks by syncing to their calendars, email and online shopping orders.

Eighteen years ago, when I first became a parent, Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care was the de facto gift to all new parents along with a Johnson & Johnson baby care set. I kept the book for a number of years after I had my second child and referred to it frequently. But today, new parents can seek advice from podcasts, influencers, online communities and yes, AI chatbots. There is a lot of advice out there, available in seconds. But how much of it is actually helping parents?

Author-editor Sanjana Kapur, 40, who’s raising a nine-year-old in Bengaluru, admits that parenting feels a little nerve-racking today. “There’s so much information out there, that you’re constantly worrying if you’re making the right decision, or how even your smallest reaction will affect your child. The world has become such a complicated place, and parents are nervous even when kids are at school now,” she admits.

"What if WhatsApp could work anywhere you go in the world without any struggle," Shah wrote, adding, "Inviting partners everywhere to join us in this important mission." WhatsApp has more than 3 billion users worldwide, according to Meta.

articles.title: Sugar restriction during first 1000 days of life reduces cancer incidence, pace of ageing: study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Reducing sugar exposure during the first 1,000 days of life is associated with a substantially lower cancer risk decades later, and a slower biological ageing process, the results of a U.K.-based study have shown.

The article , ‘ Early-life sugar restriction causally reduces adult cancer incidence and slows biological aging’ published in PNAS, analysed 64,761 adults in the U.K. Biobank, coinciding with a policy-level sugar rationing period in the U.K. People whose first 1,000 days occurred during sugar rationing had 36% to 69% lower incidence of liver/intrahepatic bile duct, rectal, prostate, breast, and lung cancers later in life. There were markers that indicated that these people had 2.2 fewer years of biological aging, and they were left with persistent healthier eating habits, even 50 years later.

articles.title: Pressure tactics: On the new U.S. tariffs on India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest U.S. tariffs on India are nothing more than a pressure tactic to push for the signing of a trade deal. The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed to levy a tariff of 25% for India’s apparent use of strategic excess manufacturing capacity to the detriment of American industry. This is the second-highest tariff rate the USTR has applied across the 14 countries that it has taken action against. The pressure on India does not come from the 25% rate but from the 17% this could be reduced to if it signs a trade deal with the U.S. This latest action is yet another example of how, despite the frothiness of India-U.S. trade relations over the past year and a half, the actual substance has not changed. The 25% rate now proposed, which is net of existing tariffs, is nearly the same as the 26% rate that U.S. President Donald Trump had first announced when he unveiled his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariffs in April 2025. Indeed, it is exactly the same as the 25% tariff he finally imposed in July 2025, before he imposed an additional 25% for India’s Russian oil imports. The 17% rate is also only marginally lower than the 18% that the two countries had agreed on in their joint statement in February 2026. It is also just one percentage point lower than the tariffs on competitors such as Indonesia and Malaysia. The allegation of India having excess capacity does not hold water. Indeed, were India to have excess manufacturing capacity in any sector, it would be the Government of India that would be the first to announce it with great fanfare, instead of denying it as it did. After all, that has been its aim since 2014.

Yet, even a basic assessment of India’s import dependence and the fact that manufacturing’s share in GDP is lower now than a decade ago shows that India is far from having excess manufacturing capacity in any sector. Further, higher tariffs are unlikely to reduce America’s imports of the goods from India that it does depend on. The USTR mentioned generic pharmaceuticals, telecommunication equipment, and renewable energy goods. The first two are items that India has developed expertise in, which is distinct from strategic excess capacity. A relatively small tariff disadvantage will not substantially erode the attractiveness of these Indian products. Renewable energy imports from India have swelled because the U.S. is reducing its purchases from China. Hanging over all of this are the 100% tariffs related to the purchase of Russian oil, which have only temporarily been paused. India has so far held off on signing a deal, and must go ahead with one only if it is convinced that the benefits at least equal the costs.

articles.summary: The latest U.S. tariffs on India are nothing more than a pressure tactic to push for the signing of a trade deal. The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed to levy a tariff of 25% for India’s apparent use of strategic excess manufacturing capacity to the detriment of American industry. This is the second-highest tariff rate the USTR has applied across the 14 countries that it has taken action against. The pressure on India does not come from the 25% rate but from the 17% this could be reduced to if it signs a trade deal with the U.S. This latest action is yet another example of how, despite the frothiness of India-U.S. trade relations over the past year and a half, the actual substance has not changed. The 25% rate now proposed, which is net of existing tariffs, is nearly the same as the 26% rate that U.S. President Donald Trump had first announced when he unveiled his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariffs in April 2025. Indeed, it is exactly the same as the 25% tariff he finally imposed in July 2025, before he imposed an additional 25% for India’s Russian oil imports. The 17% rate is also only marginally lower than the 18% that the two countries had agreed on in their joint statement in February 2026. It is also just one percentage point lower than the tariffs on competitors such as Indonesia and Malaysia. The allegation of India having excess capacity does not hold water. Indeed, were India to have excess manufacturing capacity in any sector, it would be the Government of India that would be the first to announce it with great fanfare, instead of denying it as it did. After all, that has been its aim since 2014.

articles.title: Indefensible defiance: On Tamil Nadu and Court’s Thirupparankundram order
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: By defying the Supreme Court’s one-time direction to also light the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at a stone pillar , claimed by Hindu groups to be a Deepathoon, atop the Thirupparankundram hills, the Tamil Nadu government has disregarded a constitutional body’s authority. Believed to be Lord Murugan’s first abode, the hills have, for centuries , witnessed an intersection of religious faiths, with occasional skirmishes leading to tense flare-ups and legal battles. They house the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy, Uchchi Pillaiyar and Kashi Viswanathar temples; Sultan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah; and also Jain beds. Historically, the lamp is lit near the Pillaiyar temple. In 1994-95, the Hindu Munnani precipitated matters, claiming that the moksha deepam (for departed souls) and Karthigai Deepam were being lit at the same place. It demanded the lamp be lit at a pillar, 50 metres from the Dargah. In multiple legal battles, successive governments, backed by hereditary priests (Sthaneeka Bhattars) , opposed the demand. Even in 1862 and 1912, courts had disallowed lamp lighting near the Dargah. The BJP and its affiliates have, since, aggressively weaponised the demand in the name of Hindu religious rights.

Against this backdrop, last year, the Madras High Cour t’s Madurai Bench, relying on the 1931 Privy Council ruling on ownership of the hills, held that “for the sake of protecting its property, the [Subramania Swamy] temple management is obliged to light the festival lamp at the Deepathoon” . The DMK government defied the order. Later, a Division Bench upheld the verdict. While staying this order recently, the Supreme Court cited the festival’s proximity to permit the lamp to be lit at the Deepathoon this year alone , clarifying that this did not constitute “essential religious practice”. The State filed a review petition , arguing when no right is recognised prima facie, a direction altering the existing position lacks judicial foundation. On Karthigai Deepam day, November 24, with the review pending, the government walked a tightrope. The Collector assured the High Court of compliance. Yet, the lamp was lit only at the traditional spot . The Collector has now apologised to the Court, blaming the temple’s Board of Trustees for not authorising the proposed lighting team at the Deepathoon. The administration has thus attempted to distinguish its proclaimed intent to comply with judicial directions from customs governed by the trustees. But it remains exposed to the charge of colluding with the temple authorities to breach a judicial mandate. The Deepathoon may be a mischievous prop deployed by self-serving Hindu groups, but the pillar stands on temple property. The State could have permitted the limited lighting, leaving the onus on the Court, without endorsing the Deepathoon claim or compromising religious amity. A democracy can remain healthy only when its constitutional pillars do not collide with one another.

articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Beyond generosity: on India-Nepal ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The state visit of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah to Delhi, eight months after he was voted to power as leader of the ‘GenZ’ movement that ousted the previous government, was anticipated as a chance to reset the turbulent India-Nepal relationship. Bringing Mr. Shah to India for a state visit, his first, was particularly important, given the Modi government’s tense ties with his predecessor K.P. Sharma Oli’s government; Mr. Oli was not invited to Delhi more than a year into his term and travelled to Beijing instead. Initially, Mr. Shah had also given New Delhi some worrying moments, with comments about boundary disputes, and a refusal to confirm a meeting with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, which led to the cancellation of his visit in May. Subsequently, some of the realities of governance, particularly after the massive flash flood in August , have warmed Delhi-Kathmandu relations. Following talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mr. Shah thanked India for its immediate and unstinting support in the flood relief and rescue operations. Mr. Modi’s praise for Mr. Shah indicated the forging of a personal rapport on which to build the road map for ties. India announced a Development Cooperation Package — a generous ₹15,000 crore (about $1.6 billion) — for reconstruction and long-term development in Nepal. Another announcement, to offer Nepal access to Indian ports in Gujarat and Odisha, will go a long way in helping land-locked Nepal, particularly given the bilateral bad blood over the 2015 trade blockade. The inauguration of bridges, roads, trains, energy and fuel lines, an Integrated Check post (ICP) and an agreement to set up an IIT (its third offshore campus) are all signs of concrete plans to improve relations, as outlined in the joint statement titled “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal: Re-imagining the Partnership”.

Despite some of the heated rhetoric over ties, both sides appeared to have decided to deal with areas of differences in a less public manner. Mr. Shah’s persistent comments on the boundary dispute, and long-pending request for overflight access for two debt-ridden airports, were not dealt with directly, but in a broad reference about resolving “all outstanding matters” through dialogue. While the joint statement also said they would review all bilateral treaties, New Delhi’s contention that the “Eminent Persons Group” (EPG) report that suggested important changes to the 1950 Friendship treaty, is now “not relevant”, will ruffle feathers in Kathmandu which has been keen to update the treaty. The government must remember that along with the grand gestures, it is important to keep a close eye on Nepal’s grievances as well. If disregarded, these can trip up the broader progress and conception of the bilateral relationship, as spelt out by both leaders.

articles.title: Spinning wheels: on urban mobility in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

articles.title: Mirwaiz says he was put under house arrest over Vande Mataram issue, decries action against Maulana Qasimi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Friday (November 27, 2026) said he was placed under house arrest and another prominent cleric, Maulana Rehmatullah Qasimi, was summoned to a police station over their opposition to the playing of Vande Mataram at a J&K Waqf Board function in Srinagar.

“I had anticipated that I would be punished this Friday by being put under house arrest. I also raised concerns over the recitation of Vande Mataram at the religious function of the J&K Waqf Board, as well as people’s grave concerns over the disaster-in-waiting in the ecologically fragile region of Sheshnag after the viral visuals,” the Mirwaiz said in a statement.
The Mirwaiz alleged he was “prevented from proceeding to Jama Masjid, Srinagar, to deliver the Friday sermon and offer congregational prayers.”
“It has become a precedent that every time I raise people’s issues and concerns, I am not allowed to go to Jama Masjid on that Friday,” the Mirwaiz said.
The chief cleric also expressed “deep regret” over the summoning of Mr. Qasimi, head of Kashmir’s largest seminary, Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, in Bandipora.
Mr. Qasimi also spoke about the playing of Vande Mataram during the J&K Waqf Board Day on November 23 in Srinagar, which was attended by local imams and religious scholars.

“Yesterday (Thursday), Kashmir’s renowned Islamic scholar and patron of the Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulama, Maulana Rehmatullah Qasimi Sahib, was summoned to the police station and reprimanded. Can we no longer raise our voices to safeguard our religious beliefs and sentiments? Do we not even have the right to express our religious concerns?” the Mirwaiz said.
He added that those in power must understand that “we will not tolerate any coercion in matters of faith, particularly when it comes to our fundamental belief in Tawheed.”

“It would serve the ruling regime much better if, instead of applying pressure on me, it understands the sensitivity and impact these issues have on the people of J&K. It should desist from imposing things that cause people hurt and concern,” the Mirwaiz said.

Meanwhile, Kashmir’s Grand Mufti Nasir-ul-Islam on Thursday (November 26, 2026) stated, “Reciting Vande Mataram and attending related ceremonies is not permissible under Islamic law. The act is wrong and unacceptable. Such actions should not be defended under any circumstances.”
Earlier, a number of Muslim clerics tendered apologies and offered special repentance prayers for attending the Waqf function where Vande Mataram was played.
